pageContent: An old article has been found printed on a poster from back in 1851, kindly uploaded by our readers, the text is as follows:

1st of July 1851 - The Silver Mine at Black Pine was officially declared 'Exhausted' today after no further seams have been discovered for over two months of digging.  Work is set to dismantle the extraction machinery and rails, and move along to dig out a new extraction shaft, where more seams of Silver Ore were discovered during prospecting.

images.caption: The last day of the Silver Mine at Black Pine, 30 June 1851

pageContent: John Baxley was one of the most distinguished photographers that gave up hours of his time to help our club.  Originally a Police Diver and Photographer, he was famous in his working life for working and surveying the scene for some of the most high profile cases of his time, including but not limited to the infamous unsolved Arnie Spencer Tragedy, as it came to be known.  He joined our club in 1928 following his retirement from the North West Mounties.  Here we can see John in a rare photo with the Mounties Search Party in August 1901 before starting work in the Old Silver Mine at Black Pine, he is normally on the other side of the lens!

Margaret McLeod lived a quiet and practical life in rural Ontario following her husband's retirement from the North West Mounted Police. The couple settled near Maple Grove, where Margaret became closely involved in the running of their small property.

She maintained a modest apple orchard and, during the autumn months, sold apples, preserves and other produce directly to families in the surrounding communities. The orchard was never a large commercial operation, but it became a familiar local source of fresh fruit and a modest supplement to the household income.

Margaret and William remained together on the property for the rest of their lives. She continued tending the orchard and garden after William's death in 1957, maintaining the simple rural life they had built together away from his former career on the frontier.

records.pageTitle: Local Author is heir to the Whitmore Empire
records.summary: He has it but he doesn't want it!
pageContent: Henry “Harry” Whitmore, eldest son of Sergeant Arthur Whitmore, was a lifelong resident of Saskatchewan and developed an early fascination with the caves, abandoned workings and rugged country around the Black Pine district. Unlike his father, whose career was spent in policing, Harry became known locally as an author and amateur naturalist, writing about the history, people and landscapes of the region.  But, like his father, he forewent the Whitmore & Sons family business, instead passing it to his brother Jerome in 1912 and stepping aside from the main line of heirs.

Henry became associated with the local caving clubs and took part in expeditions and informal surveys of the local cave systems, helping preserve stories and observations from an earlier generation of explorers. He was remembered as an unconventional and cheerful character, with a particular fondness for unusual clothing and spectacles, and was often described as being rather ahead of his time in his outlook. He continued writing through out his life and died around 1965.

records.pageTitle: Unexpectedly gains control of Whitmore & Sons Iron and Machinery Company
records.summary: Elder brother side steps family riches to pursue life as an Author
pageContent: Jerome Whitmore was not originally expected to take control of the family business. That distinction belonged to his elder brother Henry, who was regarded as the natural heir to the firm. However, Henry chose instead to pursue his ambitions as an author, leaving Jerome to step unexpectedly into the role. Despite the change in circumstances, Jerome proved more than capable of taking the reins, embracing the responsibilities of the Whitmore business and ensuring that the family enterprise remained firmly established in Saskatchewan.

records.pageTitle: Brian Whitmore keeps the family business alive!
records.summary: Iron industry is safe in Black Pine with Brian at the helm!
pageContent: Brian Whitmore succeeds his father, Jerome Whitmore, following his death in 1963, taking over as president of Whitmore & Sons. He continues to lead the family business today, maintaining the company's long-standing presence in Saskatchewan and keeping control firmly within Jerome's branch of the Whitmore family. Rather than returning the business to Henry Whitmore's line, Brian's succession establishes Jerome's descendants as the continuing family line behind the Whitmore enterprise. Despite his untold wealth, he remains a humble, kind man that will reach out and help the common man where it is possible to do so.
